title: Mayors on money: what fiscal devolution could mean for places like London and Teesside
label: 15 September 2026 · Fiscal devolution in England
summary: Mayors from London and Tees Valley explained how the Government’s plans to give regions more control over money might help growth, what it really means in practice, which taxes make sense to devolve, how to protect poorer areas, and how local democracy and capacity could be affected. They argued the proposals are a major step forward but warned about misunderstandings (it's often a swap of grants for tax-like payments), the need for clear equalisation rules, and risks from uneven capacity across areas.

speakers.label: Howard Dawber
speakers.name: Howard Dawber
speakers.role: Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, London City Hall

chapters.title: What ministers mean by 'fiscal devolution'
chapters.takeaway: Ministers are proposing to replace specific government grants with a single long-term payment tied to local taxes, which gives flexibility but isn't the same as full local control of tax-raising.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re here to ask whether giving mayors more control over money will boost local economies. Ben, Howard, quick introductions and then straight to the question: will this boost growth where you are?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I’m the Tees Valley mayor. A quick point: people call this 'fiscal devolution' but often it’s a change in how central money is packaged. Government can replace several grants with one block payment paid by law — technically a Section 31 grant — which is cash with fewer strings attached, not handing over full tax powers.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: I’m the Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth. Yes, it can boost growth. Example: Crossrail (now the Elizabeth line) needed funding tools like a business-rate supplement and a developer levy — if the mayor had fiscal levers earlier we could’ve acted faster. More local money control speeds up projects.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the big change is flexibility and the chance to plan longer-term rather than micro-managing multiple short grants?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Exactly. The valuable bits are flexibility and having a long-term settlement so you can plan infrastructure over 10–20 years. But remember: replacing lots of tied grants with one untied one is different from handing over real tax-setting powers.

chapters.title: Borrowing, revenue certainty and what lenders care about
chapters.takeaway: Devolved tax-like income that’s predictable lets mayors borrow for big projects, but caps, volatility and government backstops shape how much lenders will accept.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: If mayors get a named share of income tax, is that really more secure than grants? Governments can change taxes. Is the real benefit that lenders will treat a long-term tax share as collateral?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Many mayors think yes. If a payment is guaranteed in law you can borrow against it more easily. But combined authorities currently face explicit borrowing caps in their deals, so even with a steady income stream a hard cap can stop more borrowing.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London has borrowed against future transport revenues before because lenders valued the steady cashflow. Tax-backed measures like retained business rates or an overnight visitor tax look different to lenders than short-term grants. That helps projects such as rail links.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: Officials have talked about caps and collars to smooth swings — for example, if a big local employer collapses and income tax falls. Is that likely?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Treasury officials are indeed discussing caps (which limit upside) and collars (which protect on big downswings). Those details haven’t been set, but they’ll control how much risk a mayor can expose to markets.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Also note: some projects are financed by business rates and rents rather than income tax — Teesside’s SeAH deal is a good example where future business-rate and rental income supported private financing.

chapters.title: Which taxes make sense to hand to cities and why equalisation matters
chapters.takeaway: Income tax and business rates are the most sensible to devolve because they grow with the local economy and are traceable, but you must lock in a neutral baseline and protect poorer areas with a fair equalisation system.

turns.speaker: Lord Petitgas
turns.text: If you could pick ideal taxes to devolve or assign, which would you choose and why?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Four tests matter: does the tax rise with local growth; is it stable enough to plan against; can you link where it’s raised to who benefits; and will taxpayers see accountability? Income tax and business rates score well on those tests. VAT and some online taxes are messy to pin to places.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Business rates are attractive because buildings don’t move and they’re easy to measure — but be wary. If a region loses big employers, its business-rate base can fall and councils can get stuck. Any model needs floors or protections.

turns.speaker: Lord Prentis of Leeds
turns.text: If devolution is meant to reward success, how do we stop poorer areas becoming permanently worse off?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Start neutral: every area should get at least what it gets now. Convert current grants into tax shares so no one is worse off on day one. Then let places keep a share of growth above that baseline — but protect core public services and have a long reset period, say 10 years, so rewards stick.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Also consider the politics: if London keeps most of the upside and poorer places see no benefit, central government will keep stepping in. Equalisation can’t be avoided if you want a stable UK.

chapters.title: Local democracy, mayors versus councils, and planning powers
chapters.takeaway: Directly elected mayors raise public visibility and can co-ordinate across small councils, but tensions will arise over who decides planning and services — legal clarity and scrutiny arrangements are essential.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: If more power goes to mayors and combined authorities, what happens to local councils? Will mayors be able to overrule local decisions and create a democratic gap?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Different systems exist. London has a separate mayor and an elected assembly that scrutinises the mayor. Boroughs remain powerful on bins and parks. The benefit of a mayor is clearer accountability for big, cross-borough projects like transport and housing.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Outside London, combined authorities vary. Historically many mayoral powers required backing by local authority leaders. Lately more powers are becoming mayoral by design — that can feel like a shift up from local councils and will cause friction unless carefully handled.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: What about planning? London can 'call in' big developments. Is it right that mayors can override local councils on planning?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In London we use a strategic plan — the London Plan — to guide local decisions. Calling in applications is used sparingly. It works well if there’s a clear strategic policy and robust reasons; otherwise it risks centralising decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: The proposals would give other mayors similar call-in powers for big schemes. The details matter: today the consultation suggests written representations rather than public hearings for call-ins. Any mayoral decision must still be lawful and could be challenged, so you need a strong evidence base.

chapters.title: Risks, capacity gaps and next steps
chapters.takeaway: The reforms are promising but not risk-free: unequal starting points, different organisational capacity, and possible unintended shifts of powers from local councils to regions all need careful design and support.

turns.speaker: Lord Burns
turns.text: If these powers had existed 25 years ago, would regional inequality be better or worse?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: It’s complex. Teesside would have faced big swings — losing a big employer can cut revenue sharply. Devolution helps, but central government would still be the backstop in crises. The key is designing protections against boom-and-bust extremes.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Some projects could have been delivered sooner with local control, boosting growth. But international cities that do this well also face much stiffer local accountability because they can’t count on the central government to bail them out.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Ben, you said Teesside needs some extra equalisation. How would you lobby for that?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: You have to be pragmatic: if you start neutral with a transfer from richer areas, we can build capability. But the politics will be a scramble after numbers come out — places will argue for their share. That’s inevitable unless the Government sets a clear, fair formula up front.

turns.speaker: Baroness Alexander of Cleveden
turns.text: The Government paused local government reorganisation recently. Does that slow devolution?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Devolution to existing mayoralties should not be held up by wider reorganisation. Practical devolution — the money and powers for existing mayors — can proceed even while structures elsewhere are debated.

turns.speaker: Lord Reid of Cardowan
turns.text: Finally: capacity. Regions and local councils have different skills and staff. How do we avoid leaving poorer areas worse off because they lack know-how?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Capacity matters. Some combined authorities are tiny, some much larger. There will be real differences in ability to deliver big deals. Peer support between cities, targeted support from central government, and time to build teams are essential.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: London and other big cities can help share expertise. Also, the incentive to attract investment makes places build capacity quickly. But central government must back technical support, especially for regions new to financial structuring and complex negotiations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. You’ve made clear that this is a major step forward but one that needs careful design: clear rules, fair equalisation, protections against volatility, and support to build local capacity.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: If I may: this could be the biggest step in devolution since mayors began. Done right it will help places like Teesside. Done badly, it could entrench inequality or create perverse incentives. The detail and the political will matter.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: And from London’s point of view, we want to grow our economy and keep contributing to the rest of the country. The best outcome is more local control to drive growth, combined with a fair mechanism to ensure opportunity spreads across the nation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That closes the session — thank you both for a frank, practical discussion.
